```{r}
#| label: setup
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)
library(patchwork)
source(here::here("R", "wq_synthesis_helpers.R"))
source(here::here("R", "read_river_wq.R"))
source(here::here("R", "wq_target_metrics.R"))

store <- here::here("_targets")
tr <- function(x) targets::tar_read_raw(x, store = store)

chem    <- tr("lake_chem_2026")
lw      <- tr("wq_lake_long")
ann     <- tr("wq_annual")
trends  <- tr("wq_trends")
cps     <- tr("wq_changepoints")
tli     <- tr("lake_tli_annual")
ctd     <- tr("lake_ctd_2026")
ctdm    <- tr("ctd_cast_metrics")
kd      <- tr("ctd_par")
bpl     <- tr("buoy_profile_long")
be      <- tr("buoy_events")
bpd     <- tr("buoy_profile_daily")
me      <- tr("met_events")
mann    <- tr("met_annual_era5")
alum    <- tr("alum_al_daily")
alum26  <- tr("alum_dose_2026")
pcomp   <- tr("puarenga_compliance")
rwq     <- tr("river_wq_data")
rann    <- tr("river_wq_annual")
rtr     <- tr("river_wq_trends")
loads   <- tr("pc10_check_loads")
sl      <- tr("pc10_stream_loads")
pflow   <- tr("pc10_daily_flow")
dla     <- tr("driver_lake_annual")
dcor    <- tr("driver_lake_correlations")
airport <- tr("airport_met")
buoymet <- tr("all_buoy_met_data")
ctdth   <- tr("ctd_thermal")
buoyth  <- tr("buoy_thermal")
hflux   <- tr("hyp_flux")
hod     <- tr("hod_events")
hyps    <- tr("lake_hyps")
burger  <- read.csv(here::here("website", "data", "burger2007_chamber_fluxes.csv"))
enso    <- tr("enso_indices")

theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 11))
pal_site <- c("Site 2" = "#0072B2", "Site 5" = "#D55E00", "Lake (mean of sites)" = "black")
pal_layer <- c(INT = "#009E73", HYP = "#E69F00", BOT = "#CC79A7")
var_lab <- c(tp = "TP (mg/m³)", tn = "TN (mg/m³)", drp = "DRP (mg/m³)", nh4 = "NH4-N (mg/m³)",
             nnn = "NOx-N (mg/m³)", chla = "Chl-a (mg/m³)", secchi = "Secchi (m)",
             pp = "TP − DRP (mg/m³)", org_n = "Organic N (mg/m³)", tn_tp = "TN:TP (molar)",
             turb = "Turbidity (NTU)")

# Alum dosing milestones
utu_start <- as.Date("2006-06-15"); pua_start <- as.Date("2010-01-14")
pua_pause <- run_events(alum$date, alum$date > as.Date("2012-01-01") & alum$puarenga_kg_al < 1,
                        min_len = 60, max_gap = 10)
pua_pause_main <- pua_pause |> slice_max(duration, n = 1)
alum_vlines <- function(hy = TRUE) {
  x <- if (hy) c(2006.5, 2010) else c(utu_start, pua_start)
  geom_vline(xintercept = x, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50", linewidth = 0.4)
}
fmt_trend <- function(pct, p) ifelse(is.na(pct), "–",
  paste0(ifelse(p < 0.05, ifelse(pct > 0, "▲ ", "▼ "), ""), sprintf("%+.1f", pct),
         ifelse(p < 0.05, "*", "")))
```

## Key findings {#sec-summary}

```{r}
#| label: summary-numbers
lake_tli <- tli |> filter(site == "Lake (mean of sites)")
tli_last <- lake_tli |> filter(hy == max(hy))
tli_min  <- lake_tli |> filter(hy >= 2010) |> slice_min(tli3_3yr, n = 1)
tli_max  <- lake_tli |> slice_max(tli3_3yr, n = 1)
mean_int <- function(v, hys) ann |> filter(layer == "INT", variable == v, hy %in% hys) |>
  summarise(m = mean(mean)) |> pull(m)
tp_0106 <- mean_int("tp", 2001:2006); tp_1220 <- mean_int("tp", 2012:2020)
tp_2122 <- mean_int("tp", 2021:2022); tp_2326 <- mean_int("tp", 2023:2026)
tn_0106 <- mean_int("tn", 2001:2006); tn_1220 <- mean_int("tn", 2012:2020); tn_2326 <- mean_int("tn", 2023:2026)
ch_0106 <- mean_int("chla", 2001:2006); ch_1220 <- mean_int("chla", 2012:2020); ch_2326 <- mean_int("chla", 2023:2026)
```

**The lake today.** Lake Rotorua is a eutrophic, polymictic lake.

- The 3-year mean TLI3 for 2024–2026 is **`r sprintf("%.2f", tli_last$tli3_3yr)`** (hydrological year `r tli_last$hy`).
  - This is above the target of 4.2.
  - It is well below the 2004–2006 peak of `r sprintf("%.2f", tli_max$tli3_3yr)`.
  - It is higher than the 2014–2020 low of `r sprintf("%.2f", tli_min$tli3_3yr)`.
- Integrated surface-water means for 2023–2026: TP ≈ `r round(tp_2326)` mg/m³, TN ≈ `r round(tn_2326)` mg/m³, chl-a ≈ `r round(ch_2326, 1)` mg/m³.

**Three phases in the record.**

1. **Early-2000s eutrophic peak.**
   - TP ≈ `r round(tp_0106)`, TN ≈ `r round(tn_0106)`, chl-a ≈ `r round(ch_0106)` mg/m³ (2001–2006).
   - Frequent bottom-water anoxia, with summer bottom NH₄ and DRP above 400 and 50 mg/m³.
2. **Alum-era recovery, 2007 to about 2012.**
   - TP fell by about half, to ≈ `r round(tp_1220)` mg/m³ (2012–2020).
   - TN fell to ≈ `r round(tn_1220)` mg/m³ and chl-a roughly halved.
   - The step changes in TP, DRP and particulate P are detected in 2007–2010. They follow Utuhina dosing (from June 2006) and Puarenga dosing (from January 2010).
3. **A partial reversal since about 2016.** Over the last 10 years TP, TN and chl-a show significant increasing trends at both sites, and Secchi depth is decreasing at Site 5. Two things stand out:
   - **The 2020–2022 TP excursion.** Mean TP was ≈ `r round(tp_2122)` mg/m³ in 2021–2022. Bottom TP reached 160 mg/m³ and DRP 110–120 mg/m³ in summer 2021/22. Three things coincided:
     - a near-complete pause in Puarenga dosing (`r paste(format(pua_pause_main$start, "%b %Y"), "to", format(pua_pause_main$end, "%b %Y"))`);
     - the strongest lake heatwave and the longest buoy-recorded stratification (70 days, Nov 2021 – Jan 2022);
     - two low-load years (external TP ≈ 28–29 t/y).

     TP returned to about 19 mg/m³ once dosing resumed and the very wet 2023 brought a well-mixed year.
   - **Nitrogen is rising.** TN rose from about 300 to about 360 mg/m³ after 2021. This follows the high-flow 2023 and 2024 hydrological years, when modelled external TN loads were 814 and 706 t/y against the target of 435 t/y. In-lake NH₄ and NOx are also higher than in the 2010s.

**Drivers.**

- **Alum** is the strongest single correlate of lake TP and TLI (ρ ≈ −0.8). It is confounded with the time trend, but the 2019–2021 dosing pause acts as a natural experiment that supports a causal link.
- **Internal loading.** Year-to-year changes in summer air temperature track bottom-water oxygen and NH₄ accumulation. Hot, calm summers produce long stratification, anoxia and internal P and N release: 2008/09, 2010/11, 2014/15, 2017/18, 2021/22 and 2023/24.
- **Internal release rates.** The bottom layer below the thermocline (typically 9–12 m deep in summer) is only about 5 m thick on average. During stratified periods:
  - it loses oxygen at about 1.5 g O₂/m²/d (the depletion rate rises about 5 % per °C);
  - it gains NH₄ at about 25–80 mg N/m²/d and DRP at about 2–5 mg P/m²/d (lower bounds).

  These rates suggest roughly 3–15 t of DRP and 30–230 t of NH₄-N are released each summer from the deep sediments alone (@sec-internal).
- **External loads.** Wet years raise external loads (2011–2013, 2017–2018, 2023–2024) but tend to flush and mix the lake, so they reduce peak bottom DRP.
- **Warming.** The bias-corrected ERA5 record warms by about 1 °C over 1977–2025. Air-heatwave days have increased from typically 5–20 per year before 2016 to mostly 25–55 per year since then.

**Data-quality caveats.** These affect the interpretation of trends.

- The lake DRP, NH₄, NOx and TP records show changes in reporting resolution: zeros and negatives in 2015–2020, non-integer TP in 2015–2018, and finer decimals from 2021. These point to laboratory or method changes, so the "increasing DRP" trend over the last 10 years is not reliable.
- A synchronous TP rise and fall (2011–2019) across all streams, including spring-fed ones, is more likely analytical than catchment-driven.
- See @sec-dq.

## Data {#sec-data}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-inventory
#| tbl-cap: "Datasets used. All are read through the targets pipeline (`_targets.R`, section 5b)."
rng <- function(d) paste(format(min(d, na.rm = TRUE), "%Y-%m"), "to", format(max(d, na.rm = TRUE), "%Y-%m"))
tibble::tribble(
  ~Dataset, ~Content, ~Period, ~Target,
  "BOPRC lake chemistry (S2 & S5, PC10 Jun-26)", "TP, TN, DRP, NH4, NOx, TKN, chl-a, Secchi, pH, turbidity; integrated (INT), hypolimnion (HYP), bottom (BOT)", rng(chem$date), "`lake_chem_2026`",
  "BOPRC CTD profiles (S2 & S5)", "Temperature, DO, chl fluorescence, PAR, conductivity, turbidity, 1 m bins, ~monthly", rng(ctd$date), "`lake_ctd_2026`",
  "Old buoy (2007–2022) and new LERNZmp profiler (2022–)", "Daily temperature and DO profiles, 0.5 m bins; new buoy also pH, chl, turbidity, SpC, ORP", rng(bpl$date), "`buoy_profile_long`, `buoy_profile_daily`",
  "Buoy met (old + new)", "Air temp, RH, wind, rain, SW radiation", rng(as.Date(buoymet$Date)), "`all_buoy_met_data`",
  "MetService Rotorua Aerodrome", "Hourly met", rng(as.Date(airport$date)), "`airport_met`",
  "ERA5, bias-corrected to buoy/airport", "Daily air temp, rain, wind, SW, RH (continuous)", rng(me$daily$date), "`era5_corrected_daily_baseline`",
  "Alum dosing (BOPRC)", "Daily kg Al, Utuhina and Puarenga", rng(alum$date), "`alum_al_daily`",
  "Alum dose rates + Puarenga compliance", "L/day by plant; paired up/downstream TP, DRP, Al, pH", paste(rng(alum26$date), "; compliance", rng(pcomp$date)), "`alum_dose_2026`, `puarenga_compliance`",
  "BOPRC river WQ (new)", "12 sites; TN, TKN, NOx, NH4, TP, DRP, TSS, DO, pH, temp, Al, discharge", rng(rwq$date), "`river_wq_data`",
  "PC10 2026 loads (McBride 2026)", "Modelled daily flow and AED concentrations per inflow, 12 scenario sets", "1959-07 to 2026-06", "`pc10_stream_loads`, `pc10_check_loads`",
  "ENSO indices (NOAA)", "Monthly ONI, SOI, IPO, SAM",
    rng(enso$date[enso$index == "ONI"]), "`enso_indices`"
) |> kable()
```

**Notes on the data.**

- **Hydrological years.** Lake summaries use July–June hydrological years, named by the year they end. For example, 2022 is July 2021 to June 2022, and its summer is December 2021 to February 2022.
- **INT samples** are depth-integrated over the epilimnion (0 m to roughly 6–14 m).
- **BOT samples** are taken about 1 m above the sediment, at 18–22 m.
- **Trend tests** are seasonal Mann–Kendall tests on monthly medians with Sen slopes. They are not corrected for serial correlation, so p-values are optimistic.
- **Change points** are binary segmentation of deseasonalised monthly anomalies, with a conservative penalty.

**Known caveats.**

- **Site codes.** The alkalinity file uses EL805168 for Site 5, against EL802148 here.
- **Ōhau outlet record.** It may contain a lab or method change, which is not yet confirmed (see the Ōhau page).
- **Buoy met.** Units changed on 2023-10-23 (fixed in the pipeline), and buoy RH drifts.
- **Puarenga river site.** The routine site (Puarenga at FRI, EK598179) is **upstream** of the alum plant, so it does not show the effect of dosing.
- **Utuhina river site.** The Utuhina at Lake Rd site is downstream of its plant.

## In-lake nutrient chemistry {#sec-nutrients}

### Long-term patterns

```{r}
#| label: fig-annual-int
#| fig-cap: "Annual (hydrological-year) means of integrated epilimnion samples at Sites 2 and 5. Dashed lines mark the start of Utuhina (June 2006) and Puarenga (January 2010) alum dosing. Years with fewer than 6 sampled months are omitted."
#| fig-height: 8
v <- c("tp", "drp", "pp", "tn", "nh4", "nnn", "org_n", "chla", "secchi")
ann |>
  filter(layer == "INT", variable %in% v) |>
  mutate(variable = factor(var_lab[variable], var_lab[v])) |>
  ggplot(aes(hy, mean, colour = site)) +
  alum_vlines() +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 1.2) +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free_y", ncol = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal_site) +
  labs(x = "Hydrological year", y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

**Phosphorus.**

- **Before alum (1990s–2006).** Integrated TP was mostly 30–48 mg/m³. A high 1993/94 (≈ 80 mg/m³) reflects very few samples in that year.
- **Fall with dosing.** TP fell from about 40 mg/m³ in 2006 to 15–20 mg/m³ from 2011/12.
- **Composition.** DRP dropped from 5–15 mg/m³ to mostly ≤ 2 mg/m³ in the surface water. Most of the remaining TP is particulate or organic (TP − DRP), which also halved, from about 30 to 15 mg/m³.
- **2021–2022.** TP was clearly elevated (27–33 mg/m³), with DRP rising to 4–8 mg/m³. It then fell back to 18–21 mg/m³ in 2023–2026.

**Nitrogen.**

- **Peak.** TN was highest in 2000–2007 (≈ 450–575 mg/m³ at Site 2).
- **Step down.** It stepped down around 2009/10 (change point Aug 2009 at Site 2, Feb 2008 at Site 5) to about 300 mg/m³ in 2011–2021. The drop is almost all organic N (TKN − NH₄), which follows the fall in phytoplankton biomass.
- **Since 2022.** TN has risen to 340–365 mg/m³.
- **Inorganic N** is more variable:
  - NH₄ peaks in years of strong internal loading.
  - NOx-N was close to detection before 2011 and much higher afterwards: years such as 2012–2013, 2017–2018 and 2023–2024 have annual means of 40–140 mg/m³.
  - The NOx step in 2011 appears at both lake sites and, in part, in several streams. It may be partly analytical (@sec-dq), but high NOx after winter mixing is a real feature of the lake.

**Chlorophyll-a and clarity.**

- **Chl-a** peaked in 2001–2007 (20–30 mg/m³ annual means) and fell to 8–13 mg/m³ after 2012.
- **Secchi** depth improved from about 2.5 to about 3 m.
- **Last decade.** Both have edged back towards poorer conditions: chl-a 12–16 mg/m³ and Secchi 2.4–2.5 m in 2026.

### Seasonal cycle and how it has changed

```{r}
#| label: fig-seasonal
#| fig-cap: "Monthly median of integrated samples (both sites) for three periods: pre-alum, first decade of dosing, and the last decade."
#| fig-height: 6
lw |>
  filter(layer == "INT", variable %in% c("tp", "drp", "tn", "nh4", "nnn", "chla")) |>
  mutate(era = cut(date, as.Date(c("1980-01-01", "2006-07-01", "2016-07-01", "2030-01-01")),
                   labels = c("1990–2006 (pre-alum)", "2006–2016", "2016–2026")),
         month = factor(month.abb[as.integer(format(date, "%m"))], month.abb[c(7:12, 1:6)]),
         variable = factor(var_lab[variable], var_lab[c("tp", "drp", "tn", "nh4", "nnn", "chla")])) |>
  group_by(era, month, variable) |>
  summarise(med = median(value), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(month, med, colour = era, group = era)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey40", "#56B4E9", "#D55E00")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Monthly median", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5))
```

**The seasonal cycle.**

- **Late summer and autumn (Feb–May).** After stratification breaks down, nutrients released from the sediment are mixed into the surface water. TP, DRP and NH₄ peak at this time.
- **Winter and spring (Jul–Oct).** NOx-N peaks, as the NH₄ is nitrified and the lake stays mixed.

**How the cycle has changed.**

- **TP and DRP.** The late-summer and autumn TP peak (March–April) is about half of its pre-alum size (about 27 against 56 mg/m³), and similar to 2006–2016. The large autumn DRP peak of the pre-alum era (about 20 mg/m³ in March) has disappeared.
- **Ammonium.** The autumn NH₄ peak is now the largest of the three periods (median about 50 mg/m³ in April).
- **Nitrate.** The winter NOx peak (July–October, about 60–100 mg/m³) is much larger than before.
- **Nitrogen overall.** Together these suggest that N released from the sediment in summer is now mixed and nitrified in winter, rather than taken up by phytoplankton.
- **Chl-a.** It no longer shows the large summer–autumn maxima of the early 2000s, and in the last decade the seasonal range is only about 8–14 mg/m³.

### Trends

```{r}
#| label: tbl-trends
#| tbl-cap: "Seasonal Mann–Kendall trends of integrated (INT) samples, as Sen slope in % of the period median per year. ▲/▼ and * mark p < 0.05."
v <- c("tp", "drp", "pp", "tn", "nh4", "nnn", "org_n", "chla", "secchi", "tn_tp")
trends |>
  filter(layer == "INT", variable %in% v) |>
  mutate(cell = fmt_trend(pct_per_yr, p),
         variable = factor(var_lab[variable], var_lab[v]),
         period = factor(period, c("full", "pre_alum", "alum_era", "last_10y"),
                         c("1990–2026", "1990–2006", "2006–2026", "2016–2026"))) |>
  select(variable, site, period, cell) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = period, values_from = cell) |>
  arrange(variable, site) |>
  kable()
```

**What the trends show.**

- **Whole record.** TP, DRP, particulate P, TN, organic N and chl-a are all decreasing, and Secchi is increasing. This reflects the alum-era recovery.
- **Last decade (2016–2026).** The direction has reversed:
  - TP is increasing by about 2 %/yr at both sites.
  - TN is increasing by about 1.5–1.8 %/yr.
  - Chl-a is increasing by about 3–4 %/yr.
  - Secchi depth is decreasing at Site 5.
- **DRP over the last decade.** The significant DRP increase over 2016–2026 is driven by the many zero values reported in 2015–2019 (@sec-dq). It should not be read as a real increase.
- **TN:TP.** The ratio has risen from about 25 to about 40 (molar). P limitation has strengthened under alum dosing.

### Bottom waters and internal loading

```{r}
#| label: fig-bottom
#| fig-cap: "NH4-N, DRP and TP in integrated (INT), hypolimnion (HYP) and bottom (BOT) samples at Site 5 (Site 2 is similar). Bottom-water accumulation in stratified summers is the signature of internal loading."
#| fig-height: 7
lw |>
  filter(site == "Site 5", variable %in% c("nh4", "drp", "tp"), date >= as.Date("1999-07-01")) |>
  mutate(variable = factor(var_lab[variable], var_lab[c("tp", "drp", "nh4")]),
         layer = factor(layer, c("INT", "HYP", "BOT"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(date, value, colour = layer)) +
  alum_vlines(hy = FALSE) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.6, linewidth = 0.3) + geom_point(size = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~variable, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal_layer) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 years", date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = "Layer")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bottom-max
#| tbl-cap: "Annual maximum bottom-water (BOT) concentrations (mg/m³), mean of the two sites. These are a proxy for the strength of summer internal loading."
ann |>
  filter(layer == "BOT", variable %in% c("tp", "drp", "nh4")) |>
  group_by(hy, variable) |> summarise(max = round(mean(max)), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = variable, values_from = max) |>
  select(hy, tp, drp, nh4) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Hydrological year", "TP", "DRP", "NH₄-N"))
```

**Internal loading remains active.**

- Years with strong bottom-water accumulation (two-site mean of the annual bottom maxima: DRP above 50 mg/m³ and NH₄ above 400 mg/m³) are 2004, 2010, 2015, 2022 and 2025. 2016, 2021 and 2024 are close to these thresholds.
- Years with little accumulation are 2007, 2012–2014, 2017–2019, 2023 and 2026.
- **Bottom-water trends:**
  - Bottom TP and DRP have declined over the whole record, but show no decline over the last decade.
  - Bottom NH₄ has increased over the alum era at both sites (+1.8 to +4.6 %/yr).
- So alum has suppressed the P released from the sediment, but it has not removed it, and N release continues.
- The seasonal timing, the thermal controls and estimates of the release rates are in @sec-internal.

### Trophic Level Index

```{r}
#| label: fig-tli
#| fig-cap: "Annual TLI3 (chl-a, TP, TN) by site, and the lake 3-year rolling mean against the Rotorua target of 4.2. The grey line is TLI4 (including Secchi) for comparison."
lake_tli <- tli |> filter(site == "Lake (mean of sites)")
ggplot() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 4.2, linetype = 2, colour = "darkgreen") +
  alum_vlines() +
  geom_point(data = tli |> filter(site != "Lake (mean of sites)"),
             aes(hy, tli3, colour = site), size = 1.5, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_line(data = lake_tli, aes(hy, tli3_3yr), colour = "black", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(data = lake_tli, aes(hy, tli4_3yr), colour = "grey50", linewidth = 0.6) +
  annotate("text", x = 1996, y = 4.17, label = "Target 4.2", colour = "darkgreen", hjust = 0, vjust = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal_site) +
  labs(x = "Hydrological year", y = "TLI", colour = NULL)
```

**The TLI trajectory.**

- **Peak.** The 3-year TLI3 peaked at 5.0 in 2004–2006.
- **Fall.** It fell steadily with dosing, and from 2013 to 2021 it stayed close to the target (4.15–4.28).
- **Recent years.** Since 2022 it has stayed at 4.3–4.4.
  - 2022 was the TP excursion year.
  - In 2024–2026 TN is higher and chl-a is creeping up.
  - 2026 has the highest annual chl-a (≈ 16 mg/m³) since 2009.

### Data quality and laboratory changes {#sec-dq}

```{r}
#| label: fig-dq
#| fig-cap: "Reporting resolution of the integrated lake samples. Left: share of DRP values ≤ 1 mg/m³ and of zero or negative values. Right: share of TP values that are not whole numbers. Changes in either indicate method, detection-limit or laboratory changes."
#| fig-height: 4
dq <- lw |>
  filter(layer == "INT", variable %in% c("drp", "tp", "nh4", "nnn")) |>
  mutate(y = as.integer(format(date, "%Y"))) |>
  group_by(variable, y) |>
  summarise(low = mean(value <= 1), nonpos = mean(value <= 0),
            nonint = mean(abs(value - round(value)) > 1e-6), .groups = "drop")
p1 <- dq |> filter(variable == "drp") |>
  pivot_longer(c(low, nonpos)) |>
  ggplot(aes(y, value, fill = name)) + geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(low = "grey60", nonpos = "firebrick"),
                    labels = c(low = "≤ 1 mg/m³", nonpos = "≤ 0")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Share of DRP samples", fill = NULL, title = "DRP")
p2 <- dq |> filter(variable %in% c("tp", "drp", "nh4")) |>
  ggplot(aes(y, nonint, colour = variable)) + geom_line() + geom_point(size = 1) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Share non-integer", colour = NULL, title = "Reported precision")
p1 + p2
```

**Lake record.** The lake record has at least three visible reporting regimes:

1. **To about 2014.** Values are whole numbers in mg/m³, with detection limits of 0.5–1 mg/m³.
2. **2015–2020.** Many DRP values are reported as 0, with occasional −1 values in DRP, NOx and NH₄. TP is reported as non-integer values (e.g. 14.159744 and 16.113176), which look like conversions from a different unit or a different instrument.
3. **From 2021.** All nutrients are reported to 0.1 mg/m³.

**Effects on trends.**

- Trends in low-concentration surface DRP, NH₄ and NOx across these boundaries are unreliable.
- TP and TN trends are less affected, because concentrations are far above detection.

**River record.**

- TP at every stream, including the spring-fed Hamurana and Awahou streams, rises together from about 2011 and falls from about 2019 (@fig-river-anom).
- Spring-fed streams have stable, mainly geological P, so a shared step of about 20–30 % is much more likely to be analytical than a change in the catchment.
- River DRP is also high at most sites in 1993–1995 and 2003–2008, which may be a further reporting boundary.
- This matches the open question about a lab or method change in the Ōhau outlet record (labels change from "Labstar – Legacy" to "Routine" in July 2015, and grade codes change around 2020/21).
- **Recommendation:** confirm the BOPRC lab and method history (lab provider, DRP/TP methods, detection limits, censoring rules) before any trend in DRP or river TP is used in reporting or calibration.

## Buoy and CTD profiles {#sec-profiles}

### Temperature and oxygen structure

```{r}
#| label: fig-buoy-heatmap
#| fig-cap: "Weekly mean water temperature and dissolved oxygen from the old (2007–2022) and new (2022–2026) buoys, 1 m depth bins. The old buoy had thermistors at fixed depths and DO sensors only near the surface and bottom; the new profiler samples every 0.5 m. White areas are depths or periods without sensors."
#| fig-height: 7
hm <- bpl |>
  mutate(week = as.Date(cut(date, "week")), depth = round(depth_m)) |>
  group_by(week, depth) |>
  summarise(temp_c = mean(temp_c, na.rm = TRUE), do_mgl = mean(do_mgl, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(across(c(temp_c, do_mgl), \(x) ifelse(is.nan(x), NA, x)))
h1 <- ggplot(hm, aes(week, depth, fill = temp_c)) + geom_raster() +
  scale_y_reverse() + scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "C", na.value = "white") +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 years", date_labels = "%Y", expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Depth (m)", fill = "Temp (°C)")
h2 <- ggplot(hm, aes(week, depth, fill = do_mgl)) + geom_raster() +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = c("darkred", "orange", "lightyellow", "skyblue", "navy"),
                       values = scales::rescale(c(0, 2, 5, 9, 13)), limits = c(0, 14),
                       na.value = "white") +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 years", date_labels = "%Y", expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Depth (m)", fill = "DO (g/m³)")
h1 / h2
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-strat-anoxia
#| fig-cap: "Share of buoy-monitored summer days (November–March) that were stratified (surface − bottom > 1 °C), hypoxic (bottom DO < 4 g/m³) or anoxic (bottom DO < 2 g/m³), by hydrological year. Numbers are the summer days with bottom DO data."
sm <- be$daily |>
  filter(as.integer(format(date, "%m")) %in% c(11, 12, 1, 2, 3)) |>
  mutate(hy = wq_hy(date)) |>
  group_by(hy) |>
  summarise(n = sum(!is.na(do_bot)),
            Stratified = mean(d_temp > 1, na.rm = TRUE),
            Hypoxic = mean(do_bot < 4, na.rm = TRUE),
            Anoxic = mean(do_bot < 2, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(n >= 30)
sm |>
  pivot_longer(Stratified:Anoxic) |>
  mutate(name = factor(name, c("Stratified", "Hypoxic", "Anoxic"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(hy, value, fill = name)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  geom_text(data = sm, aes(hy, 1.03, label = n), inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 2.6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#56B4E9", "#E69F00", "#D55E00")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Hydrological year", y = "Share of summer days", fill = NULL)
```

**Stratification is intermittent.**

- Rotorua stratifies for days to weeks at a time between November and March, and mixes in between.
- The longest buoy-recorded stratified periods are listed below:

| Summer | Longest stratified period |
|---|---|
| 2021/22 | 70 days (8 Nov 2021 – 16 Jan 2022) |
| 2014/15 | 52 days |
| 2008/09 | 51 days |
| 2010/11 | 46 days |
| 2019/20 | 42 days |
| 2017/18 | 41 days |
| 2023/24 | 38 days |

- Bottom anoxia (DO < 2 g/m³ for at least 3 days) builds within about 1–3 weeks of stratification setting in. The longest anoxic periods are listed below:

| Period | Duration of anoxia |
|---|---|
| Jan–Feb 2015 | 30 days |
| Jan–Feb 2009 | 28 days |
| Dec 2010 | 23 days |
| Feb 2010 | 21 days |
| Jan–Feb 2018 | 18 days |
| Jan 2024 | 18 days |

- **The record is uneven.** The 2022 gap between buoys and the sparser bottom DO in 2018–2022 mean that some events (e.g. summer 2021/22) are better captured by the CTD and bottom chemistry than by the buoy.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ctd-do
#| fig-cap: "Bottom (≥ 18 m) DO and surface–bottom temperature difference from the monthly CTD casts, 2003–2026. The dashed line marks 2 g/m³."
#| fig-height: 5
c1 <- ggplot(ctdm, aes(date, do_bot, colour = site)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 2, linetype = 2) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.5) + geom_point(size = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal_site) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Bottom DO (g/m³)", colour = NULL)
c2 <- ggplot(ctdm, aes(date, d_temp, colour = site)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = 2) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.5) + geom_point(size = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal_site) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "ΔT surface − bottom (°C)", colour = NULL)
(c1 / c2) + plot_layout(guides = "collect") & theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

**CTD casts.**

- **Anoxia.** The casts confirm near-anoxic bottom water (minimum DO < 1 g/m³) in:
  - summer 2003/04 (Site 5), 2008/09 (Site 5) and 2009/10
  - summer 2015/16 (both sites at about 0.1 g/m³)
  - summer 2023/24 (Site 2, 0.7 g/m³)
- **Well-oxygenated summers.** 2011/12, 2020/21 and 2022/23 never fell below about 6 g/m³.
- **Strongest stratification.** ΔT reached 5.6–6.7 °C in summer 2017/18 and about 4 °C in 2014/15 and 2023/24.

### Light, chlorophyll and the new buoy sensors

```{r}
#| label: fig-light-chl
#| fig-cap: "Left: light attenuation Kd from CTD PAR profiles (r² > 0.8). Right: daily surface (≤ 2 m) chlorophyll fluorescence, pH, turbidity and specific conductance from the new buoy."
#| fig-height: 5
k1 <- kd |>
  ggplot(aes(Date, Kd)) + geom_point(size = 0.8, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", span = 0.3, se = FALSE, colour = "#0072B2") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Kd (m⁻¹)")
k2 <- bpd |>
  filter(depth_m <= 2) |>
  group_by(date) |>
  summarise(`Chl fluor. (RFU)` = mean(chl_fl, na.rm = TRUE), pH = mean(ph, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Turbidity (NTU)` = mean(turb, na.rm = TRUE), `SpC (µS/cm)` = mean(spcond, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  pivot_longer(-date) |>
  ggplot(aes(date, value)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~name, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
k1 + k2 + plot_layout(widths = c(1, 1.2))
```

**Light attenuation.** Kd from the CTD PAR profiles shifts in steps: about 0.35 m⁻¹ in 2003–2008, about 0.9 m⁻¹ in 2010–2016, back to about 0.35 m⁻¹ in 2020–2022, then rising again. Secchi depth improved over 2010–2016, when Kd suggests the water became darker, so these steps are more likely changes in the PAR sensor or in how the profiles were processed. Kd should not be used for trend analysis without checking the instrument history.

**New buoy, 2022–2026.**

- Surface chlorophyll fluorescence shows bloom episodes in late summer and autumn, and higher values in 2026.
- **Sensor caveats:**
  - **Conductance.** Specific conductance has a saw-tooth pattern of slow drift and abrupt steps, which matches sensor drift and recalibration at servicing rather than changes in the lake.
  - **Chlorophyll.** Fluorescence decays to a flat, low level through 2024–2025, which is typical of fouling.
  - **pH.** Surface pH drifted from about 7.5 (2022–2023) to about 6.7 (2025). This needs checking against discrete pH (see the pH page) before it is interpreted.
  - **CTD chlorophyll.** The CTD chlorophyll series also drops sharply in 2020–2021, at the same time as the drop in Kd, which suggests a sensor or calibration change rather than a real fall.
- The new-buoy data are most reliable for temperature and DO. They show bottom anoxia only in the summers of 2023/24 and 2024/25.

### Lake heatwaves

```{r}
#| label: tbl-lake-hw
#| tbl-cap: "Largest surface-water heatwaves from the buoy record (≥ 5 days above the day-of-year 90th percentile of 2007–2026). Intensity is relative to the day-of-year climatology."
be$heatwaves |>
  arrange(desc(max_anom)) |> head(12) |>
  transmute(Start = start, End = end, Days = duration, `Max temp (°C)` = round(max_temp, 1),
            `Max anomaly (°C)` = round(max_anom, 1), Category = category) |>
  kable()
```

**The strongest lake heatwaves.**

- December 2017 (20 days, +3.9 °C)
- Christmas 2021 to January 2022 (19 days, "strong")
- November 2025
- January 2024 and January 2015 (both coinciding with long anoxic periods)

The highest surface temperatures in the buoy record are 24–24.7 °C, in summer 2015/16, 2017/18, 2021/22 and 2023/24.

## Internal loading {#sec-internal}

Lake Rotorua is polymictic. It does not stratify through the whole summer like a deep monomictic lake. Instead it stratifies for days to weeks at a time between about October and March, and wind events mix it in between. Each stratified period isolates a thin bottom layer, roughly 3–8 m thick, over the deep sediments. That layer loses oxygen quickly and gains NH₄ and DRP released from the sediment. The next mixing event carries those nutrients into the surface water. This section uses the temperature profiles (buoys and CTD), the bottom-water chemistry and the lake hypsography to describe this cycle and to estimate the release rates.

### Seasonal cycle of stratification

```{r}
#| label: fig-thermal-season
#| fig-cap: "Seasonal cycle of thermal structure from the daily buoy profiles (2007–2026). Lines are the median by week of year and ribbons the 25–75th and 10–90th percentiles: surface–bottom temperature difference, Schmidt stability (from the lake hypsograph), thermocline depth (on stratified days only, ΔT ≥ 1 °C, searched between 3 m and 2 m above the bed), and bottom (≥ 18 m) DO. Weeks are ordered July–June."
#| fig-height: 8
bdaily <- buoyth |>
  group_by(date) |>
  summarise(d_temp = mean(d_temp), schmidt = mean(schmidt), thermo_depth = mean(thermo_depth, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(thermo_depth = ifelse(is.nan(thermo_depth), NA, thermo_depth)) |>
  left_join(be$daily |> select(date, do_bot), by = "date")
wk_order <- c(27:53, 1:26)
season_q <- bdaily |>
  mutate(wk = pmin(as.integer(format(date, "%U")) + 1, 53),
         wk = match(wk, wk_order)) |>
  pivot_longer(c(d_temp, schmidt, thermo_depth, do_bot)) |>
  filter(is.finite(value)) |>
  group_by(name, wk) |>
  summarise(q10 = quantile(value, .1), q25 = quantile(value, .25), q50 = median(value),
            q75 = quantile(value, .75), q90 = quantile(value, .9), n = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(n >= 10) |>
  mutate(name = factor(name, c("d_temp", "schmidt", "thermo_depth", "do_bot"),
                       c("ΔT surface − bottom (°C)", "Schmidt stability (J/m²)",
                         "Thermocline depth (m)", "Bottom DO (g/m³)")))
mlab <- tibble::tibble(wk = c(1, 5.4, 9.8, 14.1, 18.5, 22.8, 27.1, 31.5, 35.8, 40.2, 44.5, 48.9),
                       lab = month.abb[c(7:12, 1:6)])
ggplot(season_q, aes(wk)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q10, ymax = q90), fill = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q25, ymax = q75), fill = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(aes(y = q50), colour = "#0072B2") +
  geom_hline(data = tibble::tibble(name = factor("Bottom DO (g/m³)", levels(season_q$name)), y = 2),
             aes(yintercept = y), linetype = 2, colour = "firebrick") +
  facet_wrap(~name, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = mlab$wk, labels = mlab$lab) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-thermal-month
#| tbl-cap: "Monthly summary of thermal structure from the buoys (daily) and CTD casts (monthly, Sites 2 and 5): share of days or casts stratified (ΔT ≥ 1 °C), median thermocline depth on stratified days, and median Schmidt stability."
mon <- function(d) d |> mutate(m = factor(month.abb[as.integer(format(date, "%m"))], month.abb[c(7:12, 1:6)])) |>
  group_by(m) |>
  summarise(strat = mean(d_temp >= 1), zth = median(thermo_depth[d_temp >= 1], na.rm = TRUE),
            ss = median(schmidt), .groups = "drop")
left_join(mon(bdaily), mon(ctdth), by = "m", suffix = c("_buoy", "_ctd")) |>
  transmute(Month = m, `Stratified (buoy)` = scales::percent(strat_buoy, 1),
            `Thermocline, m (buoy)` = round(zth_buoy, 1), `Schmidt, J/m² (buoy)` = round(ss_buoy, 1),
            `Stratified (CTD)` = scales::percent(strat_ctd, 1),
            `Thermocline, m (CTD)` = round(zth_ctd, 1)) |>
  kable()
```

**When the lake stratifies.**

- Stratification starts to develop in October and November.
- It is most frequent and strongest from December to February. On about half of all summer days the surface is at least 1 °C warmer than the bottom, and Schmidt stability on calm, hot days exceeds 100–300 J/m².
- It collapses in March as the lake cools. From April to August the lake is fully mixed.
- **Thermocline depth.** On stratified days the thermocline is typically 9–12 m deep (monthly medians; interquartile range about 7–13 m). The isolated bottom layer therefore covers roughly a third to half of the lake bed, because the hypsograph is steep below 10 m.
- **The bottom layer is thin.** Its mean thickness (hypolimnion volume divided by its sediment area) is only about 4–6 m. A thin layer over a large sediment area is why oxygen falls so fast: below 2 g/m³ within 1–3 weeks of the onset of stratification.

### Stratified periods and the thermocline, summer by summer

```{r}
#| label: fig-thermo-summers
#| fig-cap: "Daily thermocline depth from the buoys (points, only on stratified days), coloured by bottom DO, for each summer (November–March). Grey shading marks days with bottom DO < 2 g/m³. Gaps are periods without a thermocline (mixed) or without data."
#| fig-height: 10
sdat <- bdaily |>
  filter(as.integer(format(date, "%m")) %in% c(11, 12, 1, 2, 3)) |>
  mutate(summer = paste0(wq_hy(date) - 1, "/", substr(wq_hy(date), 3, 4)),
         doy = as.numeric(date - as.Date(paste0(wq_hy(date) - 1, "-11-01"))))
ggplot(sdat, aes(doy)) +
  geom_rect(data = \(d) filter(d, do_bot < 2), aes(xmin = doy - 0.5, xmax = doy + 0.5, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf),
            fill = "grey80") +
  geom_point(aes(y = thermo_depth, colour = do_bot), size = 0.7) +
  scale_y_reverse(limits = c(20, 0)) +
  scale_colour_gradientn(colours = c("darkred", "orange", "gold", "skyblue", "navy"),
                         values = scales::rescale(c(0, 2, 4, 7, 11)), limits = c(0, 11),
                         na.value = "grey50") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 30, 61, 92, 120), labels = c("Nov", "Dec", "Jan", "Feb", "Mar")) +
  facet_wrap(~summer, ncol = 4) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Thermocline depth (m)", colour = "Bottom DO\n(g/m³)")
```

**Summer by summer.** The summers differ mainly in how long the stratified periods last and how often wind breaks them up.

- **Long stratified periods with prolonged bottom anoxia:** 2007/08, 2008/09, 2014/15, 2015/16, 2017/18 and 2023/24. In these summers the thermocline deepens steadily, by about 1 m a week, from 6–9 m to 12–16 m as the period goes on.
- **Long stratification without bottom-DO data:** 2019/20 and 2021/22 (grey points). The bottom chemistry shows strong accumulation in both.
- **Short stratified periods separated by frequent mixing, with little anoxia:** 2011/12, 2012/13, 2013/14, 2016/17, 2022/23 and 2025/26.
- **Missing:** the 2009/10 and 2010/11 summers are largely missing from the buoy record.
- **New profiler (from 2022).** Thermocline depths are similar to the old buoy's: a median of about 10 m in November–December and about 13 m in January.

### Seasonal cycle of bottom-water nutrients

```{r}
#| label: fig-int-load-season
#| fig-cap: "Monthly medians (both sites) of NH4-N, DRP and TP in the bottom (BOT), hypolimnion (HYP) and integrated (INT) samples, for the pre-alum period, the first decade of dosing and the last decade. The lower panels show the bottom − integrated difference: the excess that internal loading builds up below the thermocline."
#| fig-height: 9
era_cut <- function(date) cut(date, as.Date(c("1980-01-01", "2006-07-01", "2016-07-01", "2030-01-01")),
                              labels = c("1990–2006 (pre-alum)", "2006–2016", "2016–2026"))
lm_ <- lw |>
  filter(variable %in% c("nh4", "drp", "tp")) |>
  mutate(era = era_cut(date),
         month = factor(month.abb[as.integer(format(date, "%m"))], month.abb[c(7:12, 1:6)]),
         variable = factor(var_lab[variable], var_lab[c("nh4", "drp", "tp")]))
p_a <- lm_ |>
  group_by(era, layer, month, variable) |>
  summarise(med = median(value), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(layer = factor(layer, c("INT", "HYP", "BOT"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(month, med, colour = layer, group = layer)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 0.8) +
  facet_grid(variable ~ era, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal_layer) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Monthly median (mg/m³)", colour = "Layer") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, size = 7))
p_b <- lm_ |>
  filter(layer %in% c("BOT", "INT")) |>
  group_by(era, site, date, month, variable, layer) |>
  summarise(value = mean(value), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = layer, values_from = value) |>
  filter(is.finite(BOT), is.finite(INT)) |>
  group_by(era, month, variable) |>
  summarise(excess = median(BOT - INT), q75 = quantile(BOT - INT, .75), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(month, excess, colour = era, group = era)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey40", "#56B4E9", "#D55E00")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "BOT − INT (mg/m³)", colour = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, size = 7), legend.position = "bottom")
p_a / p_b + plot_layout(heights = c(2.2, 1))
```

**The internal-loading signal follows stratification closely.**

- The bottom-water excess over the surface water (BOT − INT) is near zero from April to September.
- It builds from November or December and peaks in January–February, which is the timing of the longest stratified, anoxic periods.
- It collapses again in March as the stratification breaks down. In the integrated surface samples, the released NH₄ and P then appear as the March–May peaks in @fig-seasonal.

**Before and after alum.**

- **Before alum,** the median December–March bottom DRP excess was 12–18 mg/m³.
- **Since 2006,** it has been 0–5 mg/m³.
- **NH₄** shows no such fall. Its summer bottom excess in 2016–2026 (up to about 210 mg/m³ in January) is larger than before alum, and it starts earlier, from November.
- **TP.** The TP excess in 2016–2026 is again larger than in 2006–2016.
- **Reading.** This pattern supports the view that alum caps the release of P from the sediment, but does not reduce the mineralisation of organic matter that supplies N.

### Stratification strength and internal loading, year by year

```{r}
#| label: fig-strat-vs-load
#| fig-cap: "Summer (December–February) stratification strength from the buoys against the annual maximum bottom-water concentrations (mean of Sites 2 and 5). Labels are hydrological years; colour separates years before full dosing of both streams (≤ 2010) from later years."
#| fig-height: 4.5
sstrat <- bdaily |>
  filter(as.integer(format(date, "%m")) %in% c(12, 1, 2)) |>
  mutate(hy = wq_hy(date)) |>
  group_by(hy) |>
  summarise(n = n(), schmidt = mean(schmidt), strat_days = sum(d_temp >= 1) * 90 / n(),
            anox_days = sum(do_bot < 2, na.rm = TRUE) * 90 / sum(is.finite(do_bot)), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(n >= 45)
bmax <- ann |> filter(layer == "BOT", variable %in% c("drp", "nh4")) |>
  group_by(hy, variable) |> summarise(max = mean(max), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = variable, values_from = max)
sv <- inner_join(sstrat, bmax, by = "hy") |> mutate(period = ifelse(hy <= 2010, "≤ 2010", "2011–2026"))
sv |>
  pivot_longer(c(drp, nh4), names_to = "var", values_to = "max") |>
  mutate(var = c(drp = "Bottom DRP max (mg/m³)", nh4 = "Bottom NH4 max (mg/m³)")[var]) |>
  pivot_longer(c(schmidt, strat_days), names_to = "x", values_to = "xv") |>
  mutate(x = c(schmidt = "Mean summer Schmidt stability (J/m²)",
               strat_days = "Stratified days, Dec–Feb (scaled to 90)")[x]) |>
  ggplot(aes(xv, max, label = hy, colour = period)) +
  geom_text(size = 2.7) +
  geom_smooth(aes(group = 1), method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "grey50", linewidth = 0.4) +
  facet_grid(var ~ x, scales = "free") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("≤ 2010" = "grey40", "2011–2026" = "#D55E00")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: strat-load-cor
ct_ <- function(x, y) { k <- suppressWarnings(cor.test(x, y, method = "spearman")); sprintf("ρ = %.2f, p = %.2f", k$estimate, k$p.value) }
r_drp_ss <- ct_(sv$schmidt, sv$drp); r_nh4_ss <- ct_(sv$schmidt, sv$nh4)
r_drp_sd <- ct_(sv$strat_days, sv$drp); r_nh4_sd <- ct_(sv$strat_days, sv$nh4)
```

**Year-to-year links between stratification and bottom concentrations.** These use the `r nrow(sv)` hydrological years with buoy coverage.

- **NH₄:**
  - against mean summer Schmidt stability, `r r_nh4_ss`
  - against stratified days, `r r_nh4_sd`
- **DRP:**
  - against Schmidt stability, `r r_drp_ss`
  - against stratified days, `r r_drp_sd`

**How to read these.**

- The relationships are weakly positive (ρ ≈ 0.4 with Schmidt stability, p ≈ 0.1) and essentially absent for the count of stratified days. Monthly bottom samples catch the peak of each event only by chance, and the strength of stratification matters more than its duration.
- For DRP, the alum era shifts the response downwards. For the same stratification, post-2010 years mostly have lower bottom DRP, with the exceptions of 2015, 2021, 2022 and 2025.
- 2021/22 stands out as high stratification combined with very high DRP, in the year the Puarenga dosing was paused.

### Estimating release rates (fluxes)

Two independent estimates are possible from the monitoring data. Both are compared with the sediment-chamber fluxes measured in the lake by Burger et al. (2007) and with the values in the model's `aed.nml`.

**1. Hypolimnetic accumulation (NH₄, DRP, TP).**

- **Which samples are used.** Pairs of consecutive monthly samples at the same site when the CTD casts show the lake stratified on both dates.
- **Hypolimnetic mass.** The mean of the HYP and BOT samples multiplied by the volume below the thermocline (from the hypsograph, using the mean thermocline depth of the two casts).
- **Flux.** The change in that mass divided by the time between samples and by the sediment area below the thermocline.
- **These are lower bounds.** The lake mixes partially between monthly samples, so some released mass is lost upward. Positive intervals are summarised below.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-hyp-flux
#| tbl-cap: "Hypolimnetic accumulation fluxes (mg/m²/d) from consecutive stratified CTD and chemistry sampling dates, 2003–2026. n is the number of sample pairs; positive pairs are those where the hypolimnetic mass increased."
hflux |>
  group_by(Variable = c(nh4 = "NH4-N", drp = "DRP", tp = "TP")[variable]) |>
  summarise(`Pairs (n)` = n(), `Positive` = sum(flux > 0),
            `Median of positive` = median(flux[flux > 0]),
            `75th pct of positive` = quantile(flux[flux > 0], .75),
            `Max` = max(flux),
            `Thermocline (m)` = median(z_th), `Mean hypolimnion thickness (m)` = median(h_mean),
            `Interval (d)` = median(days)) |>
  kable(digits = 1)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-hyp-flux
#| fig-cap: "Hypolimnetic accumulation fluxes for each pair of stratified sampling dates, against mean bottom temperature. Open symbols are negative (net loss, usually partial mixing between samples)."
#| fig-height: 4
hflux |>
  mutate(variable = factor(c(nh4 = "NH4-N", drp = "DRP", tp = "TP")[variable], c("NH4-N", "DRP", "TP")),
         sign = ifelse(flux > 0, "gain", "loss")) |>
  ggplot(aes(t_bot, flux, colour = site, shape = sign)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(gain = 16, loss = 1)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal_site) +
  labs(x = "Bottom temperature (°C)", y = "Flux (mg/m²/d)", colour = NULL, shape = NULL)
```

**2. Hypolimnetic oxygen depletion (from the buoys).**

- **Which periods are used.** Each buoy-recorded stratified period (at least 7 days) that starts with bottom DO above 2 g/m³.
- **Volumetric rate.** A regression of daily bottom DO against time, up to the point where DO first falls below 1 g/m³.
- **Areal hypolimnetic oxygen demand (AHOD).** The volumetric rate multiplied by the mean hypolimnion thickness below the median thermocline depth of the period.
- **What it measures.** AHOD is a measure of total sediment and hypolimnetic oxygen demand. It is directly comparable with chamber sediment oxygen demand (SOD).

```{r}
#| label: fig-hod
#| fig-cap: "Hypolimnetic oxygen depletion in buoy-recorded stratified periods. Left: volumetric rate against mean bottom temperature, with an exponential (θ) fit. Right: areal hypolimnetic oxygen demand (AHOD) by year, with the interquartile range of the Burger et al. (2007) light-chamber SOD (grey band)."
#| fig-height: 4
hod_ok <- hod |> filter(rate > 0, r2 >= 0.5)
th_fit <- lm(log(rate) ~ I(t_bot - 20), data = hod_ok)
theta <- exp(coef(th_fit)[2]); r20 <- exp(coef(th_fit)[1])
h1 <- ggplot(hod_ok, aes(t_bot, rate)) + geom_point() +
  geom_line(data = tibble::tibble(t_bot = seq(10, 23, 0.1)) |> mutate(rate = r20 * theta^(t_bot - 20)),
            colour = "#D55E00") +
  labs(x = "Mean bottom temperature (°C)", y = "DO decline (g/m³/d)")
h2 <- ggplot(hod_ok, aes(start, ahod)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = quantile(burger$sod_g_m2_d[burger$chamber == "light"], .25),
           ymax = quantile(burger$sod_g_m2_d[burger$chamber == "light"], .75), fill = "grey85") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = t_bot)) + scale_colour_viridis_c(option = "C") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "AHOD (g O₂/m²/d)", colour = "T bottom (°C)")
h1 + h2
```

```{r}
#| label: flux-numbers
ahod_med <- median(hod_ok$ahod); ahod_iqr <- quantile(hod_ok$ahod, c(.25, .75))
rate_med <- median(hod_ok$rate)
# Redfield mineralisation: 138 mol O2 : 16 mol N : 1 mol P
gN_per_gO2 <- 16 * 14.007 / (138 * 31.998); gP_per_gO2 <- 30.974 / (138 * 31.998)
pos <- function(v) median(hflux$flux[hflux$variable == v & hflux$flux > 0])
```

**Oxygen depletion results.**

- Across `r nrow(hod_ok)` well-fitted stratified periods (r² ≥ 0.5), bottom DO fell at a median `r sprintf("%.2f", rate_med)` g/m³/d.
- The median AHOD is **`r sprintf("%.1f", ahod_med)` g O₂/m²/d** (interquartile range `r sprintf("%.1f–%.1f", ahod_iqr[1], ahod_iqr[2])`).
- The depletion rate rises with bottom temperature, with θ ≈ `r sprintf("%.3f", theta)` per °C. That is about `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * (theta^5 - 1))` % faster at 20 °C than at 15 °C. This is one mechanism by which warmer summers strengthen internal loading.
- The AHOD values sit within the chamber SOD range of Burger et al. (2007), 0.3–4.0 g O₂/m²/d in the light chambers. They are towards the upper part of it, which is expected, because AHOD also includes oxygen demand in the water column below the thermocline.

**Converting oxygen demand to nutrient release.** If the oxygen demand were all due to the mineralisation of Redfield organic matter (O₂:N:P = 138:16:1 by mole), the median AHOD would correspond to:

- about **`r sprintf("%.0f", ahod_med * 1000 * gN_per_gO2)` mg N/m²/d**
- about **`r sprintf("%.1f", ahod_med * 1000 * gP_per_gO2)` mg P/m²/d**

This is an upper-bound-type estimate for N. For P it is an estimate of mineralisation only. It excludes P released when iron oxides are reduced, which can be larger, and it excludes the P bound by alum.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-flux-compare
#| tbl-cap: "Comparison of internal-load flux estimates for Lake Rotorua (mg/m²/d, O₂ in g/m²/d). Chamber values are the range of the light-chamber means of Burger et al. (2007), 2003–2004, at 7–20 m depth. The aed.nml values are the current model settings (three sediment zones)."
bl <- burger |> filter(chamber == "light")
fmt_r <- function(x, d = 0) paste(formatC(min(x), format = "f", digits = d), "–", formatC(max(x), format = "f", digits = d))
tibble::tribble(
  ~Method, ~`NH4-N`, ~`DRP / SRP`, ~`O2 demand`,
  "Hypolimnetic accumulation, this study (median of positive intervals; lower bound)",
    sprintf("%.0f", pos("nh4")), sprintf("%.1f", pos("drp")), "–",
  "Hypolimnetic accumulation, 75th percentile / max",
    sprintf("%.0f / %.0f", quantile(hflux$flux[hflux$variable == "nh4" & hflux$flux > 0], .75), max(hflux$flux[hflux$variable == "nh4"])),
    sprintf("%.1f / %.1f", quantile(hflux$flux[hflux$variable == "drp" & hflux$flux > 0], .75), max(hflux$flux[hflux$variable == "drp"])), "–",
  "Oxygen depletion (AHOD), buoys, median",
    sprintf("%.0f (Redfield)", ahod_med * 1000 * gN_per_gO2), sprintf("%.1f (Redfield)", ahod_med * 1000 * gP_per_gO2),
    sprintf("%.1f", ahod_med),
  "Burger et al. 2007 chambers (light, 7–20 m)",
    paste(fmt_r(bl$nh4_phase2_mg_m2_d), "(phase 2);", fmt_r(bl$nh4_phase1_mg_m2_d), "(phase 1)"),
    fmt_r(bl$srp_mg_m2_d, 1), fmt_r(bl$sod_g_m2_d, 2),
  "Model aed.nml (fsed_amm, fsed_frp, fsed_oxy; zones 1–3)",
    paste(sprintf("%.0f", c(6.654, 2.408, 0.616) * 14.007), collapse = ", "),
    paste(sprintf("%.1f", c(0.0602, 0.0657, 0.0254) * 30.974), collapse = ", "),
    paste(sprintf("%.2f", c(30.1, 30.1, 23.33) * 31.998 / 1000), collapse = ", ")
) |> kable()
```

**How the estimates compare.**

- **NH₄.**
  - The accumulation estimates (median about 25 mg N/m²/d, up to about 80) are at the low end of the chamber rates (33–224 mg N/m²/d in the secondary phase).
  - The oxygen-demand-based estimate (about 78 mg N/m²/d) sits within them.
  - Together they put summer NH₄ release in Rotorua at roughly **25–100 mg N/m²/d**, so the model's zone-1 value (about 93 mg N/m²/d) is plausible.
  - The two deeper zones (34 and 9 mg N/m²/d) look low.
- **DRP.**
  - Accumulation (2004–2024) gives about 2–5 mg P/m²/d (maximum about 8 mg P/m²/d, in 2019/20 and 2020/21).
  - That is at the lower end of the 2003–2004 chamber range (2–86 mg P/m²/d in the light chambers), which was measured before alum dosing.
  - The model's `fsed_frp` (0.8–2 mg P/m²/d) is at or below the lowest observed value. It may be too low unless the model supplies P to the sediment by another route (settling and mineralisation, or the alum-bound pool).
- **Oxygen.** AHOD (interquartile range about 1.0–2.1 g O₂/m²/d) is consistent with the chamber SOD. It is above `fsed_oxy` (0.75–0.96 g O₂/m²/d), but the difference is mostly accounted for by water-column demand below the thermocline.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-internal-annual
#| tbl-cap: "Order-of-magnitude summer internal load: release rate × sediment area below the median summer thermocline × stratified days (December–February, buoy). Low uses the median hypolimnetic accumulation flux and high the 75th percentile (DRP), or the Redfield-equivalent of AHOD (NH4). Compare with the external loads (alum_storm_central)."
a_sed <- hyps_area(hyps, median(bdaily$thermo_depth[as.integer(format(bdaily$date, "%m")) %in% c(12, 1, 2)], na.rm = TRUE))
q_drp <- quantile(hflux$flux[hflux$variable == "drp" & hflux$flux > 0], c(.5, .75))
f_nh4 <- c(pos("nh4"), ahod_med * 1000 * gN_per_gO2)
ext <- loads |> filter(scenario == "alum_storm_central") |> select(hy, ext_tp = tp, ext_tn = tn)
sstrat |>
  inner_join(ext, by = "hy") |>
  transmute(`Hydrological year` = hy, `Stratified days` = round(strat_days),
            `DRP (t P)` = sprintf("%.1f–%.1f", strat_days * a_sed * q_drp[1] / 1e9, strat_days * a_sed * q_drp[2] / 1e9),
            `External TP (t/y)` = round(ext_tp, 1),
            `NH4-N (t N)` = sprintf("%.0f–%.0f", strat_days * a_sed * f_nh4[1] / 1e9, strat_days * a_sed * f_nh4[2] / 1e9),
            `External TN (t/y)` = round(ext_tn)) |>
  kable()
```

**Scaling up to an annual internal load.**

- Sediment area below the median summer thermocline: about `r sprintf("%.0f", a_sed / 1e6)` km².
- Release rates:
  - DRP: `r sprintf("%.1f–%.1f", q_drp[1], q_drp[2])` mg/m²/d
  - NH₄: `r sprintf("%.0f–%.0f", f_nh4[1], f_nh4[2])` mg N/m²/d

**What the scaling suggests.**

- **P.** Each summer's stratified periods release in the order of 3–15 t of DRP in most years, against an external TP load of about 28–60 t/y. It was lowest in the barely stratified 2009/10 (about 1–2 t) and highest in 2021/22 (about 7–16 t).
- **N.** NH₄-N release is in the order of 30–230 t, against an external TN load of 380–815 t/y.

**Limits of these totals.**

- They cover only the stratified bottom layer in December–February.
- They exclude release during mixed periods. Burger et al. (2007) found SRP release largely independent of DO.
- They exclude release from the shallower sediments, which occupy the larger area.

So these are conservative. Earlier whole-lake budgets put internal loading at a substantial share of the total P load. These monitoring-based rates are best treated as the floor of the range the model's sediment fluxes should reproduce.


## Sudden changes and events {#sec-events}

### Event definitions {#sec-event-defs}

All events are detected automatically from continuous daily series (functions in `R/wq_synthesis_helpers.R`; targets `met_events` and `buoy_events`).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-event-defs
#| tbl-cap: "Definitions of the events used in this report."
st_thr <- attr(me$storms, "threshold_mm")
tibble::tribble(
  ~Event, ~`Data`, ~Definition, ~`Number detected`,
  "Air heatwave", "ERA5-BC daily mean air temperature, 1976–2026",
    "At least 5 consecutive days above the day-of-year 90th percentile (11-day window, 1991–2020 baseline); gaps of up to 2 days are bridged. This is the Hobday et al. (2016) marine-heatwave definition applied to air temperature.",
    sprintf("%d (%d since 2016)", nrow(me$air_heatwaves), sum(me$air_heatwaves$start >= as.Date("2016-01-01"))),
  "Lake (surface) heatwave", "Buoy daily mean water temperature at ≤ 1.5 m, 2007–2026",
    "Same rule as for air heatwaves, applied to lake surface temperature (cf. Woolway et al. 2021). The climatology uses the whole buoy record, because the record is too short for a 30-year baseline.",
    sprintf("%d", nrow(be$heatwaves)),
  "Heatwave category", "Both",
    "The peak anomaly expressed in multiples of the threshold-minus-climatology difference on that day: 1–2× Moderate, 2–3× Strong, 3–4× Severe, ≥ 4× Extreme (Hobday et al. 2018).",
    "–",
  "Storm (heavy-rain event)", "ERA5-BC daily rainfall, 1976–2026",
    sprintf("The 3-day running rainfall total exceeds its 99th percentile (%.0f mm); exceedances within 3 days of each other are one event. The event magnitude is the largest 3-day total. The peak modelled total inflow (PC10 loads) is reported alongside.", st_thr),
    sprintf("%d (%d since 2016)", nrow(me$storms), sum(me$storms$start >= as.Date("2016-01-01"))),
  "Stratified", "Buoy and CTD profiles",
    "The surface (≤ 1.5 m) minus bottom (≥ 18 m) temperature is ≥ 1 °C. Stratified periods are runs of at least 3 such days (gaps of up to 2 days bridged).",
    sprintf("%d periods", nrow(be$stratified)),
  "Bottom anoxia / hypoxia", "Buoy bottom (≥ 18 m) DO",
    "Bottom DO below 2 g/m³ (anoxia) or below 4 g/m³ (hypoxia) for at least 3 days (gaps of up to 2 days bridged).",
    sprintf("%d anoxic periods", nrow(be$anoxia))
) |> kable()
```

### Examples

```{r}
#| label: hw-daily
air_hw <- detect_heatwaves(me$daily$date, me$daily$tair, base_years = 1991:2020)
hw_example <- function(daily, events, from, to, title, ylab) {
  d <- daily |> filter(date >= as.Date(from), date <= as.Date(to))
  ev <- events |> filter(end >= as.Date(from), start <= as.Date(to))
  ggplot(d, aes(date)) +
    geom_rect(data = ev, aes(xmin = start - 0.5, xmax = end + 0.5, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf),
              inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = "#F4A582", alpha = 0.5) +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = thresh, ymax = pmax(temp, thresh)), fill = "#B2182B", alpha = 0.6) +
    geom_line(aes(y = clim), colour = "grey40", linetype = 2) +
    geom_line(aes(y = thresh), colour = "grey40") +
    geom_line(aes(y = temp), colour = "black", linewidth = 0.4) +
    scale_x_date(date_labels = "%d %b\n%Y") +
    labs(x = NULL, y = ylab, title = title)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-ex-air-hw
#| fig-cap: "Air heatwave examples (ERA5-BC daily mean air temperature, black). The dashed line is the day-of-year climatology (1991–2020), the solid grey line the 90th-percentile threshold, red fill the exceedance and pink bands the detected heatwave periods. Left: the 21-day summer heatwave of December 2021 – January 2022 (Strong). Right: the August 2022 winter heatwave (Severe), when temperatures were near summer values."
#| fig-height: 3.8
ev_a <- me$air_heatwaves
hw_example(air_hw$daily, ev_a, "2021-11-15", "2022-02-15", "Summer 2021/22", "Air temperature (°C)") +
  hw_example(air_hw$daily, ev_a, "2022-07-15", "2022-09-30", "Winter 2022", NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-ex-lake-hw
#| fig-cap: "Lake (surface water) heatwave examples from the buoys, same layout as the air-heatwave figure. Left: December 2017, the most intense lake heatwave on record (+3.9 °C above climatology, 20 days), which coincided with 41 days of stratification and bottom anoxia. Right: Christmas 2021 – January 2022 (Strong, 19 days), at the end of the 70-day stratified period of summer 2021/22."
#| fig-height: 3.8
hw_example(be$heatwave_daily, be$heatwaves, "2017-11-01", "2018-02-28", "Summer 2017/18", "Surface water temperature (°C)") +
  hw_example(be$heatwave_daily, be$heatwaves, "2021-11-01", "2022-02-28", "Summer 2021/22", NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-ex-storm
#| fig-cap: "Storm examples. Top: ERA5-BC daily rainfall (bars) and 3-day running total (line), with the 99th-percentile 3-day threshold (dashed) and detected storm events (blue bands). Bottom: modelled total inflow to the lake (PC10 loads, all inflows) and daily mean wind speed. Left: late January and February 2023 (the late-January storm and Cyclone Gabrielle). Right: the July 2025 storm sequence, including the second-largest 3-day total in the record."
#| fig-height: 6
storm_example <- function(from, to, title) {
  rr <- me$daily |> arrange(date) |>
    mutate(roll3 = as.numeric(stats::filter(rain_mm, rep(1, 3), sides = 1))) |>
    filter(date >= as.Date(from), date <= as.Date(to))
  ev <- me$storms |> filter(end >= as.Date(from), start <= as.Date(to))
  q <- pflow |> filter(inflow == "All inflows", date >= as.Date(from), date <= as.Date(to))
  p1 <- ggplot(rr, aes(date)) +
    geom_rect(data = ev, aes(xmin = start - 0.5, xmax = end + 0.5, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf),
              inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = "#92C5DE", alpha = 0.5) +
    geom_col(aes(y = rain_mm), fill = "#2166AC", width = 0.8) +
    geom_line(aes(y = roll3), colour = "black") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = st_thr, linetype = 2, colour = "firebrick") +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Rain (mm/d; 3-day total)", title = title)
  p2 <- ggplot() +
    geom_line(data = q, aes(date, flow_m3s), colour = "#0072B2") +
    geom_line(data = rr, aes(date, wind * 5), colour = "grey50", linetype = 2) +
    scale_y_continuous(sec.axis = sec_axis(~ . / 5, name = "Wind (m/s, dashed)")) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Total inflow (m³/s)")
  p1 / p2 + plot_layout(heights = c(1.4, 1))
}
(storm_example("2023-01-10", "2023-03-10", "Jan – Feb 2023") |
   storm_example("2025-06-20", "2025-08-20", "Jul 2025"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-ex-summer
#| fig-cap: "Anatomy of one summer, 2017/18: air temperature (ERA5-BC) with air-heatwave periods, buoy surface and bottom water temperature with lake-heatwave periods, bottom DO with anoxic periods (< 2 g/m³), and daily rainfall with storm events. Shaded bands mark the detected events in each panel."
#| fig-height: 8
from <- as.Date("2017-11-01"); to <- as.Date("2018-03-31")
band <- function(ev, fill) {
  ev <- ev |> filter(end >= from, start <= to)
  geom_rect(data = ev, aes(xmin = start - 0.5, xmax = end + 0.5, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = fill, alpha = 0.4)
}
w <- \(d) filter(d, date >= from, date <= to)
x_sc <- scale_x_date(limits = c(from, to), date_breaks = "1 month", date_labels = "%b %Y")
e1 <- ggplot(w(me$daily), aes(date, tair)) + band(me$air_heatwaves, "#F4A582") +
  geom_line() + x_sc + labs(x = NULL, y = "Air temp (°C)")
e2 <- be$daily |> w() |> select(date, Surface = t_surf, Bottom = t_bot) |>
  pivot_longer(-date) |>
  ggplot(aes(date, value, colour = name)) + band(be$heatwaves, "#D6604D") +
  band(be$stratified, "grey85") + geom_line() + x_sc +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Surface = "#D55E00", Bottom = "#0072B2")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Water temp (°C)", colour = NULL) + theme(legend.position = c(0.9, 0.25))
e3 <- ggplot(w(be$daily), aes(date, do_bot)) + band(be$anoxia, "#B2ABD2") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 2, linetype = 2, colour = "firebrick") +
  geom_line(colour = "purple4") + x_sc + labs(x = NULL, y = "Bottom DO (g/m³)")
e4 <- ggplot(w(me$daily), aes(date, rain_mm)) + band(me$storms, "#92C5DE") +
  geom_col(fill = "#2166AC") + x_sc + labs(x = NULL, y = "Rain (mm/d)")
e1 / e2 / e3 / e4
```

**What the examples show.**

- **Air heatwaves** in Rotorua typically peak 2–6 °C above the climatology and last 1–3 weeks. Since 2016 they have occurred in winter as well as summer. August 2022 was the most intense ("Severe"), with daily means near 15 °C.
- **Lake surface heatwaves** follow air heatwaves combined with light winds.
  - The December 2017 event warmed the surface to about 23 °C while the bottom stayed near 16 °C.
  - It set up a 41-day stratified period, and bottom DO fell from about 10 g/m³ to below 2 g/m³ in about four weeks.
- **Mixing ends the anoxia.** Mixing in late December, then the storm of early January 2018 (149 mm in 3 days, daily mean wind up to 14 m/s), reoxygenated the bottom water. A hot spell then re-stratified the lake: a second lake heatwave in late January brought the surface to 24.7 °C, and anoxia returned within two weeks.
- **Storms** are mostly 2–4-day events, and the modelled total inflow responds within a day.
  - **Late January 2023:** inflow peaked at 83 m³/s and stayed above about 25 m³/s for three weeks.
  - **Cyclone Gabrielle:** more rain (229 mm in 3 days), and the windiest of the large storms (daily mean wind about 15 m/s), but a smaller modelled inflow peak (about 34 m³/s).
  - **The July 2025 sequence:** three storms in five weeks, ending with the second-largest 3-day total on record (285 mm) and an inflow peak of about 60 m³/s.


### Detected change points

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cps
#| tbl-cap: "Change points in the mean of deseasonalised monthly series (binary segmentation, ≥ 24-month segments), integrated samples. Values are segment means in mg/m³ (Secchi in m)."
cps |>
  filter(layer == "INT") |>
  mutate(variable = var_lab[variable], cp = format(cp_date, "%b %Y"),
         across(c(mean_before, mean_after, delta), \(x) signif(x, 3))) |>
  select(Variable = variable, Site = site, `Change at` = cp, Before = mean_before,
         After = mean_after, Change = delta) |>
  arrange(Variable, Site) |>
  kable()
```

**The change points group into a few episodes.**

1. **1996–2002.** TN, chl-a and organic N increase. This is the late-1990s deterioration that led to the 2000s blooms.
2. **2007–2010.** TP, DRP and particulate P fall, and TN, chl-a and organic N fall about a year later. This follows the start of dosing at Utuhina in 2006 and Puarenga in 2010.
3. **2011.** A step up in NOx at both sites, with a similar step in several streams in April 2011. It may be partly analytical.
4. **2019–2021.** A step up in TP (Jun–Nov 2020) and DRP (2019–2021), reversed in late 2022. This aligns with the Puarenga dosing pause.
5. **2015 and 2021–2023.** Steps up in TN and NH₄ (bottom NH₄ from Jan 2015; INT NH₄ Apr 2021; TN Jul 2021 and Feb 2023).

### Event timeline

```{r}
#| label: fig-timeline
#| fig-cap: "Lake response (top: monthly mean integrated TP and bottom DRP, both sites) against events (bottom): ERA5-BC storms (3-day rain > 99th percentile; size = total), air heatwaves, lake heatwaves, buoy anoxic periods and alum dosing gaps."
#| fig-height: 8
x0 <- as.Date("2003-01-01")
resp <- lw |>
  filter(date >= x0, (layer == "INT" & variable == "tp") | (layer == "BOT" & variable == "drp")) |>
  mutate(m = as.Date(format(date, "%Y-%m-01")),
         series = ifelse(variable == "tp", "INT TP", "BOT DRP")) |>
  group_by(series, m) |> summarise(value = mean(value), .groups = "drop")
pt <- ggplot(resp, aes(m, value, colour = series)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("INT TP" = "#009E73", "BOT DRP" = "#CC79A7")) +
  scale_x_date(limits = c(x0, as.Date("2026-07-01")), date_breaks = "2 years", date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "mg/m³", colour = NULL) + theme(legend.position = "top")
seg <- bind_rows(
  me$air_heatwaves |> transmute(start, end, type = "Air heatwave"),
  be$heatwaves |> transmute(start, end, type = "Lake heatwave"),
  be$anoxia |> transmute(start, end, type = "Bottom anoxia (buoy)"),
  pua_pause |> transmute(start, end, type = "Puarenga dosing paused")
) |> filter(end >= x0)
st <- me$storms |> filter(peak_date >= x0)
pe <- ggplot() +
  geom_segment(data = seg, aes(x = start, xend = end + 3, y = type, yend = type, colour = type),
               linewidth = 5) +
  geom_point(data = st, aes(peak_date, "Storm (3-day rain)", size = total_mm),
             colour = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Air heatwave" = "orange", "Lake heatwave" = "firebrick",
                                 "Bottom anoxia (buoy)" = "purple",
                                 "Puarenga dosing paused" = "grey40"), guide = "none") +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 6) +
  scale_x_date(limits = c(x0, as.Date("2026-07-01")), date_breaks = "2 years", date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, size = "Rain (mm)")
pt / pe + plot_layout(heights = c(1.3, 1))
```

### Storm events and the lake response

```{r}
#| label: tbl-storms
#| tbl-cap: "Largest 3-day rainfall events in the bias-corrected ERA5 record since 2000, with the modelled peak total inflow (PC10 loads) within ±3 days."
allin <- pflow |> filter(inflow == "All inflows")
me$storms |>
  filter(peak_date >= as.Date("2000-01-01")) |>
  arrange(desc(total_mm)) |> head(15) |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(peak_q = max(allin$flow_m3s[abs(as.numeric(allin$date - peak_date)) <= 3])) |>
  ungroup() |>
  transmute(`Peak day` = peak_date, `3-day rain (mm)` = round(total_mm),
            `Max daily rain (mm)` = round(max_day_mm), `Max daily wind (m/s)` = round(max_wind, 1),
            `Peak inflow (m³/s)` = round(peak_q, 1)) |>
  kable()
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-storm-response
#| tbl-cap: "Lake response to large storms: anomaly (relative to the site-and-month median) of the first integrated sample within 45 days after each of the 40 largest 3-day rain events since 1995, against the anomaly of all other samples."
int <- lw |> filter(layer == "INT", variable %in% c("tp", "drp", "tn", "nnn", "chla", "turb")) |>
  mutate(month = as.integer(format(date, "%m"))) |>
  group_by(site, variable, month) |> mutate(anom = value - median(value)) |> ungroup()
big <- me$storms |> filter(peak_date >= as.Date("1995-01-01")) |> slice_max(total_mm, n = 40)
post <- bind_rows(lapply(big$peak_date, function(d) {
  int |> filter(date > d, date <= d + 45) |>
    group_by(site, variable) |> slice_min(date, n = 1) |> ungroup() |> mutate(storm = d)
}))
resp_tab <- int |>
  mutate(after_storm = paste(site, variable, date) %in% paste(post$site, post$variable, post$date)) |>
  group_by(variable, after_storm) |>
  summarise(n = n(), med_anom = median(anom), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = after_storm, values_from = c(n, med_anom))
wt <- int |>
  mutate(after_storm = paste(site, variable, date) %in% paste(post$site, post$variable, post$date)) |>
  group_by(variable) |>
  summarise(p = tryCatch(wilcox.test(anom[after_storm], anom[!after_storm])$p.value,
                         error = function(e) NA_real_))
resp_tab |> left_join(wt, by = "variable") |>
  transmute(Variable = var_lab[variable], `n after storm` = n_TRUE,
            `Median anomaly after storm` = signif(med_anom_TRUE, 2),
            `Median anomaly otherwise` = signif(med_anom_FALSE, 2), `p (Wilcoxon)` = signif(p, 2)) |>
  kable()
```

**Large storms.**

- The largest storms in the continuous record are:
  - July 2004
  - late July 2025 (285 mm in 3 days)
  - May 2010
  - January 2011
  - Cyclone Gabrielle (13–14 February 2023)
  - April 2017 (two events)
  - March 2016
- **Flows.** Modelled total inflow peaked at 97 m³/s on 29 April 2018 and 83 m³/s on 28 January 2023, the highest since the 1960s.

**Lake response.**

- **No consistent spike.** Monthly sampling seldom catches storm effects. Across 40 large storms, the first sample after a storm was not significantly different in TP, DRP, TN or turbidity. Chl-a was slightly higher (median +1.1 mg/m³, p ≈ 0.05).
- **Lasting effects.** These come through the annual loads and through mixing:
  - The wet years 2011–2013, 2017–2018 and 2023–2024 carried 40–60 t/y of TP and 570–815 t/y of TN (alum_storm_central), well above the PC10 targets.
  - The cool, windy and wet summer of 2022/23 (the Gabrielle summer) had little stratification, well-oxygenated bottom water and the lowest bottom DRP of the decade.
  - The large N load of 2023–2024 is the most likely source of the higher TN and NOx in 2023–2026.

### Case studies

**2009/10 – 2010/11: the last high-internal-load period before full dosing.**

- Long stratification (51 days in summer 2008/09, 46 days in 2010/11) brought repeated anoxia.
- Bottom DRP reached 116 mg/m³ and NH₄ 732 mg/m³ at Site 5 in 2010.
- Full dosing on both streams from 2011 (88–100 t Al/y) was followed by the lowest TP (13–17 mg/m³) and TLI on record in 2012–2013, despite the wet, high-load years 2011–2013.

**2014/15 and 2015/16: hot summers under dosing.**

- 2015 had the 30-day anoxic period, and bottom DRP and NH₄ returned to 56–78 and 490–670 mg/m³.
- Surface TP stayed near 20 mg/m³.
- Internal release persisted under dosing, but was not mixed into the epilimnion in large amounts.

**2019–2022: dosing pause, heat and drought.**

- **Dosing pause.** Puarenga dosing dropped to 6.5 t Al in 2018/19 and to zero in 2019/20, and resumed during 2020/21.
- **Weather.**
  - 2019 was very dry (794 mm), and 2019 and 2020 were warm and sunny.
  - 2020/21 and 2021/22 had the lowest external TP loads since the 1990s (28–29 t/y).
  - Summer 2021/22 brought an air heatwave (21 days, Dec 2021 – Jan 2022), a strong lake heatwave and 70 days of stratification.
- **Lake response.**
  - Bottom DRP reached 108–118 mg/m³ and TP 157–162 mg/m³.
  - Surface DRP and TP rose to the highest values since 2010.
- **Reading.** With external loads at a minimum, this points to an internal source. The sediment P was no longer being capped by Puarenga alum, and was then released under strong, long stratification.
- **Recovery.** TP fell back in 2022/23, after the resumption of dosing (64 t Al from Puarenga in 2022/23) and in a cool, wet, well-mixed summer.

**2023 – 2026: wet years, high N loads, rising TN and chl-a.**

- 2023 was the wettest year in the ERA5 record (2478 mm), followed by an above-average 2024.
- The 2023 TN load (814 t/y) was the highest since 1990, and 2024 (706 t/y) was also well above the target.
- Lake TN, NH₄ and NOx rose, and in 2026 chl-a rose and Secchi depth fell.
- TP has stayed near 19–21 mg/m³ under steady dosing (50–96 t Al/y).

## Observational drivers {#sec-drivers}

### Meteorology

```{r}
#| label: fig-met-compare
#| fig-cap: "Annual (hydrological-year) mean air temperature from bias-corrected ERA5, the Rotorua Aerodrome (MetService) and the lake buoys. Years with < 85 % coverage are omitted."
ap <- airport |>
  mutate(hy = wq_hy(as.Date(date))) |>
  group_by(hy) |> summarise(tair = mean(temperature_c, na.rm = TRUE), n = sum(!is.na(temperature_c))) |>
  filter(n > 0.85 * 8760) |> mutate(source = "Aerodrome")
bm <- buoymet |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(Date)) |>
  group_by(date) |> summarise(t = mean(MET_tmpair, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  filter(is.finite(t)) |>
  mutate(hy = wq_hy(date)) |>
  group_by(hy) |> summarise(tair = mean(t), n = n()) |>
  filter(n > 0.85 * 365) |> mutate(source = "Buoy")
bind_rows(mann |> transmute(hy, tair, source = "ERA5-BC"), ap, bm) |>
  ggplot(aes(hy, tair, colour = source)) + geom_line() + geom_point(size = 1) +
  geom_smooth(data = \(d) filter(d, source == "ERA5-BC"), method = "lm", se = FALSE,
              linetype = 2, linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("ERA5-BC" = "black", Aerodrome = "#E69F00", Buoy = "#0072B2")) +
  labs(x = "Hydrological year", y = "Mean air temperature (°C)", colour = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-met-anom
#| fig-cap: "Bias-corrected ERA5 anomalies relative to 1991–2020: annual air temperature, annual rain, summer (DJF) wind speed and summer shortwave radiation, and annual air-heatwave days. Shading shows the mean Oceanic Niño Index (ONI) of each hydrological year (red El Niño, blue La Niña)."
#| fig-height: 8
oni <- enso |> filter(index == "ONI") |> mutate(hy = wq_hy(as.Date(date))) |>
  group_by(hy) |> summarise(oni = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE))
base <- mann |> filter(hy %in% 1991:2020)
hwd <- me$air_heatwaves |> mutate(hy = wq_hy(start)) |> group_by(hy) |> summarise(v = sum(duration))
an <- mann |>
  transmute(hy, `Air temp (°C)` = tair - mean(base$tair),
            `Rain (% of mean)` = 100 * (rain_mm / mean(base$rain_mm) - 1),
            `Summer wind (m/s)` = wind_djf - mean(base$wind_djf, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Summer SW (W/m²)` = swr_djf - mean(base$swr_djf, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  left_join(hwd, by = "hy") |> mutate(`Air heatwave days` = coalesce(v, 0)) |> select(-v) |>
  pivot_longer(-hy) |> left_join(oni, by = "hy") |>
  mutate(name = factor(name, c("Air temp (°C)", "Rain (% of mean)", "Summer wind (m/s)",
                               "Summer SW (W/m²)", "Air heatwave days")))
ggplot(an, aes(hy, value)) +
  { if (nrow(oni)) geom_tile(aes(y = 0, height = Inf, fill = oni), alpha = 0.35, width = 1) } +
  geom_col(width = 0.7, fill = "grey25") +
  facet_wrap(~name, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166AC", mid = "white", high = "#B2182B", limits = c(-2, 2),
                       oob = scales::squish) +
  labs(x = "Hydrological year", y = NULL, fill = "ONI")
```

**Agreement between sources.** The buoy and aerodrome records agree with the bias-corrected ERA5 on year-to-year variability. The bias correction was fitted to them, so this is expected.

**What the continuous ERA5-BC record shows.**

- **Warming.** About +1 °C from the late 1970s to the 2020s. 2019–2025 are among the warmest years, and 2022 is the warmest (14.6 °C).
- **Heatwaves.** A step-like increase in air-heatwave days after 2016, to mostly 25–55 days per hydrological year. Before then it was typically 5–20 days, with peaks in 1990, 1998–1999 and 2011.
- **Rain.** Large swings: dry 2015 and 2019, against very wet 2010–2011, 2017 and 2022–2023.
- **ENSO.** La Niña years (2011–2012, 2021–2023) tend to be warm and humid, sometimes wet.
- **Calm spells.** Summer wind has no clear trend. The calmest summers (2014/15 and 2017/18) match the longest stratification and the largest surface–bottom temperature differences.

### Alum dosing

```{r}
#| label: fig-alum
#| fig-cap: "Annual aluminium dosed (t Al per hydrological year; 2026 is to February only) by stream, and daily dose rates 2022–2026 (L alum/day)."
#| fig-height: 6
a1 <- alum |>
  mutate(hy = wq_hy(date)) |>
  group_by(hy) |>
  summarise(Utuhina = sum(utuhina_kg_al) / 1000, Puarenga = sum(puarenga_kg_al) / 1000) |>
  pivot_longer(-hy) |>
  ggplot(aes(hy, value, fill = name)) + geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Utuhina = "#56B4E9", Puarenga = "#E69F00")) +
  labs(x = "Hydrological year", y = "t Al", fill = NULL)
a2 <- alum26 |>
  select(date, Puarenga = puarenga_l_d, Utuhina = utuhina_l_d) |>
  pivot_longer(-date) |>
  ggplot(aes(date, value, colour = name)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Utuhina = "#56B4E9", Puarenga = "#E69F00")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Alum (L/day)", colour = NULL)
a1 / a2
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-compliance
#| tbl-cap: "Puarenga compliance monitoring, August 2025 – July 2026: paired samples upstream (EK598179, Puarenga @ FRI) and downstream (EK637325) of the dosing plant. Medians (mg/L)."
pcomp |>
  group_by(Position = position) |>
  summarise(n = n(), pH = median(ph, na.rm = TRUE), TP = median(tp, na.rm = TRUE),
            DRP = median(drp, na.rm = TRUE), Al = median(al, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  mutate(across(TP:Al, \(x) signif(x, 3))) |>
  kable()
```

**History of dosing.**

- **Utuhina.** About 13–38 t Al/y since mid-2006.
- **Puarenga.** About 40–75 t Al/y from 2011 to 2018. This was cut to 6.5 t in 2018/19 and to zero in 2019/20, then resumed part-way through 2020/21 (20 t), peaking at 64 t Al in 2022/23 (the year after the TP excursion).
- **Total.** Dosing peaked at 101 t Al/y in 2011/12 and was 96 t Al/y in 2022/23.

**Compliance monitoring (2025–2026).**

- Dosing lowers Puarenga DRP by about 70 %, from a median of 0.031 to 0.009 mg/L.
